title: Foreign Keys and Referential Integrity
relevance: Campus OAs and SDE interviews use foreign keys to check whether candidates understand how relational constraints keep cross-table references valid.

phases.goal: Establish what a foreign key is and how referenced vs referencing relations enforce referential integrity.

must_hit.point: A foreign key is an attribute or set of attributes that references the primary key of the same relation or another relation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate defines FK as a reference to a primary key, possibly including self-reference.

must_hit.point: Referential integrity guarantees that a reference always points at something that exists.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states the integrity goal as no dangling references to missing keys.

must_hit.point: The referenced relation is the parent/base table whose primary key is pointed at; the referencing relation is the child table that holds the foreign key.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate correctly labels parent vs child roles for a Student/Course-style example.

probes: What is a foreign key, and how does it relate to referential integrity?

hints.1: Think about how one table’s column can point at another table’s key.
hints.2: Name the two roles: the table being pointed at versus the table holding the pointer.
hints.3: A foreign key references a primary key so every reference must point at an existing row.

phases.goal: Pin down which insert/delete/update operations can violate referential integrity and what ON DELETE actions do.

must_hit.point: On the referenced (parent) table, insert never violates; delete and update of the referenced key may violate.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says adding a parent is safe, but deleting or updating the parent key can orphan children.

must_hit.point: On the referencing (child) table, insert and update may violate; delete never violates.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says a bad child FK insert/update can dangle, while deleting a child cannot break the link.

must_hit.point: When a parent delete or key update would orphan children, the FK can specify ON DELETE CASCADE, ON DELETE SET NULL, or ON DELETE NO ACTION (the default, which rejects the operation).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate lists cascade, set null, and no action/reject as the referential actions.

probes: Which operations on the parent and child tables can violate referential integrity, and what happens on parent delete?

hints.1: Ask which side of the link you are changing: parent key or child foreign key.
hints.2: Parent insert and child delete are always safe; the risky cases are child insert/update and parent delete/key update.
hints.3: Parent delete is handled by CASCADE (delete children), SET NULL (null the FK), or NO ACTION (reject).

phases.goal: Contrast the three referential actions when a parent delete would orphan child rows.

must_hit.point: ON DELETE CASCADE deletes the dependent child rows along with the parent.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says cascade removes matching children automatically.

must_hit.point: ON DELETE SET NULL sets the children’s foreign-key value to null instead of deleting them.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says children remain but their FK becomes null.

must_hit.point: ON DELETE NO ACTION rejects the parent operation and is the default behaviour.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate identifies reject/fail as the default when orphans would result.

probes: If deleting a parent would orphan children, how do CASCADE, SET NULL, and NO ACTION differ?

hints.1: Focus only on what happens to child rows when the parent is deleted.
hints.2: One option removes children, one nulls the FK, one blocks the delete.
hints.3: CASCADE deletes dependents; SET NULL nulls the FK; NO ACTION rejects (default).

phases.goal: Apply the asymmetry to the classic exam pattern and the SQL insert-into-child failure.

must_hit.point: If a is a foreign key in R1 referencing the primary key of R2, then insert into R1 and delete from R2 can violate referential integrity; insert into R2 and delete from R1 cannot.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate maps R1=referencing and R2=referenced and answers insert into R1 plus delete from R2.

must_hit.point: Inserting a child row whose foreign key has no matching parent is rejected (e.g., Oracle ORA-02291: parent key not found); ON DELETE CASCADE does not help that case.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains child insert fails when parent is missing, and cascade only affects parent deletes.

probes: Given R1 referencing R2, which of insert/delete on each relation can violate referential integrity?

hints.1: Identify which relation holds the foreign key and which holds the primary key.
hints.2: Violations come from inserting into the referencing relation or deleting from the referenced relation.
hints.3: Answer is insert into R1 and delete from R2; child insert with a missing parent still fails even with ON DELETE CASCADE.

tradeoffs.topic: ON DELETE CASCADE vs ON DELETE SET NULL vs ON DELETE NO ACTION
tradeoffs.strong_answer: CASCADE deletes dependent child rows with the parent; SET NULL keeps child rows but nulls their foreign key; NO ACTION rejects the parent operation and is the default.

gotchas.trap: Assuming ON DELETE CASCADE also fixes inserting a child whose parent key is missing.
gotchas.correction: CASCADE only governs parent delete (or key update) by removing children; a child insert with no matching parent still violates referential integrity (e.g., ORA-02291).

gotchas.trap: Thinking every insert or delete on either table can violate referential integrity.
gotchas.correction: Inserting into the referenced (parent) table and deleting from the referencing (child) table never violate; danger is child insert/update and parent delete/key update.
